articles.title: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
articles.content: I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again. Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP —hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis , which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4 —a lower bound (!!) , matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6. There are two separate shocks here. The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3 (he got ω≤log 2 7) … and that the true answer is actually a rational number (!). But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to prove any lower bound of the form ω>2. I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP. Over the decades, I often heard colleagues express extreme confidence that ω=2, and I expressed skepticism whenever this came up—not because I had any strong argument for ω>2, but just because I saw that there was no strong argument for ω=2 either. So, I’m glad to have been vindicated about that ! But wait, there was more. During dessert, we saw another OpenAI release proving that the true number of linear gates needed to compute the Fourier Transform is N (log N) 1/2+o(1) . The upper bound here improves, not only over the O(N log N) that stood since the 1960s (i.e., the Fast Fourier Transform or FFT), but also over the O(N log 0.9999999999999 N) (give or take some 9’s) that OpenAI published back in the October 6 Mathocalypse. Again, though, the real shock here is that there’s also a matching lower bound (!!) . All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting … straight-up answered , rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues. To give an idea of how much things have changed, the other day Yupan Liu put a preprint on the arXiv proving that QIP(2) = PSPACE —that is, quantum interactive protocols with only two messages have the full power of those with three, or any polynomial number. As recently as 2025, this would’ve considered been one of the top complexity results of the year, and the fact that Yupan had used AI to help achieve it would’ve been strange and wonderful. These days, I had to remind myself it had even happened, and the use of AI was so standard that it didn’t even raise an eyebrow. It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the s

articles.title: 1Password Security Incident
articles.content: The short version An attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including the names and email addresses that customers use to sign into 1Password. Your vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected. 1Password does not have access to your password or secret keys. We implemented containment measures, restored clean versions of the affected service, and have triggered a rotation of internal credentials. You do not need to update anything in your 1Password account. We recommend being cautious of phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails about 1Password, such as invitations or account recovery requests that you did not initiate. 1Password apps and services are working normally. What happened On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker. What information was affected The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include: Names and email addresses Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security) Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account) Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers) The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security. When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning . During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. articles.content: [<prev] [next>] [day] [month] [year] [list] Message-ID: <20261125172638.73c0a05b@hboeck.de> Date: Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:26:38 +0100 From: Hanno Böck <hanno@...eck.de> To: oss-security@...ts.openwall.com Subject: Slow Ubuntu security response times Hello, Lately, I'm observing that Ubuntu's response to severe security flaws is concerning. On November 16th, details about a remote memory corruption called NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288) in the Linux kernel's TCP stack were published: https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/11/15/2 Today, nine days later, Ubuntu still has not published a fix yet: https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-99288 Other distros had a fix already available when the details were published. Likewise, a KVM host escape (CVE-2026-99312) affecting AMD virtualization published on Nov 18th has no fix yet either [3]: https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-99312 Ubuntu has been slow in patching another remote TCP corruption (CVE-2026-98432) lately, where it took multiple weeks until a fix was available. See also: https://chalmovsky.com/posts/wtf-ubuntu Recent news indicates that this is might be exploited in the wild: https://www.greynoise.io/blog/check-point-security-management-servers-intrusion-campaign I think everyone understands that these times aren't easy for security teams. Nevertheless, remote corruption vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel are the kind of thing where I expect updates to be available within hours, not days or weeks. On a recent Ubuntu LTS system, the kernel version is 7.0.0-44. This seems to indicate that Ubuntu is not relying on longterm supported kernels from kernel.org, but is instead backporting patches to an old kernel version. On a Debian stable system, the kernel version is 6.12.118+deb13, indicating that it's based on a very recent longterm kernel from kernel.org. I would consider the backporting strategy for the kernel to be hardly viable and probably everyone should base their Linux kernels on longterm releases supported by the Linux kernel developers. -- Hanno Böck - Independent security researcher https://itsec.hboeck.de/ https://badkeys.info/ Powered by blists - more mailing lists Please check out the Open Source Software Security Wiki , which is counterpart to this mailing list . articles.title: Much shorter version of GRH Lean verification from Anthropic
articles.content: GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, in Lean 4 Research artifact. Not maintained and not accepting contributions. A Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, built on Mathlib and using only the axioms propext , Classical.choice and Quot.sound . The proof is based on Levent Alpöge's, with Claude ( https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf ). This repository is a shorter version, produced in collaboration with my colleagues at Anthropic, and Claude. grh/ : readable edition, about 300,000 lines. Start at grh/GUIDE.md . grh-compact/ : the same five theorems, about 76,000 lines. Each folder is its own Lake project with its own README. Needs Lean v4.35.0 and Mathlib at commit 56a00585. In either folder: lake exe cache get lake build lake env lean scripts/PrintAxioms.lean A build takes one to two hours on 12 cores with 24 GB of memory (about 85 minutes more if the Mathlib cache is missing). The proof has passed machine checks only, listed in each folder's README. No mathematician has read it through, and no paper comes with it. Apache 2.0, Copyright 2026 Anthropic, PBC. See LICENSE , and NOTICE and ATTRIBUTION.md in each folder.

articles.title: A few questions for the guy who went snorkeling in a Home Depot retention pond
articles.content: One night earlier this fall, a biologist and YouTuber in Florida named Joseph Ricketts went snorkeling in a retention pond next to his local Home Depot. He filmed what he saw and posted a video to his channel titled “ Night Snorkel In a Home Depot Retention Pond .” It quickly blew up, hitting more than 2 million views as of this writing, and for good reason: It’s not at all what you might expect. Ricketts found an aquatic world teeming with life on his dive into what is, from the surface, a stagnant pool of water filled with old beer cans. A water snake undulated through the pond, a bulge in its stomach revealing a recent meal. Tadpoles darted about, some of them half on their way to froghood. Mysterious shrimp scuttled along the silty bottom. Ricketts, who works as a crocodile and alligator research biologist in Florida, went for his first snorkeling trip when he was 16 years old. On that trip, he came face-to-face with a manatee — and was instantly hooked. “I experienced so much joy in that moment, and I just kind of subconsciously knew I’d be chasing that for the rest of my life to some degree or another,” he told me. Ricketts still takes a lot of joy in snorkeling, in part because of how it allows him to quickly access a totally different world hiding just under the surface of the water; his YouTube bio declares, “I’ll snorkel pretty much anywhere.” And his recent retention pond dive among the suburban detritus bears that out. I talked with Ricketts recently about urban ecology, snorkeling, and what motivates a person to jump into the pond behind the Home Depot three miles from his house (his shortest-ever commute to a dive yet). Our interview has been edited for length and clarity. That’s a good question. I’m scuba certified, and I enjoy anything underwater, but snorkeling is just super accessible. I have a camera housing and a wet suit and other gear, but really all you need is just a mask and snorkel. As long as the water’s not freezing cold, you can get in there and take a look around. I really enjoy how, as soon as you immerse your head, it feels like you’re in a totally different world. But the beautiful thing is that you’re not. You’re in the same world, it’s just this is the one that you didn’t have a vision into before. It’s kind of a meditative, calming practice. Just taking a look around at what is happening in nature and how things survive in their own environment is pretty awesome. I love it. I honestly had the idea for it a couple years ago. I’d see people out there birding with binoculars and telephoto lenses, and I started wondering if I could snorkel in there. We’ve had a drought so I couldn’t do it for a really long time, and when we finally got some rain I decided to go for it. Tell me about the retention pond. articles.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
articles.content: The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads , two of the Times ’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.” Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT ’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view , which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes. It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times , where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.” In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps , which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge , which reiterated the policy outlined in the email. It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge ’s request for more information. Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT .

articles.title: Nfs2root: A 12-year-old pre-auth remote root in the Linux kernel's NFS server
articles.content: Port 2049 sits open on file servers, NAS appliances, build farms and Kubernetes storage nodes. Since 2014, the Linux kernel listening on it has let anyone who can reach it write into kernel memory before logging in. We pointed OpenSec's Antara at it. It came back with a root shell. CVSS 9.8 critical Advisory CVE-2026-99362 critical CVSS 9.8 Pre-auth heap overflow in the Linux NFS server (nfsd) Fixed in Linux 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1. Update the kernel and reboot. What you need to know What: a pre-auth heap overflow in the kernel's NFS server, nfsd . Who: any Linux host serving NFSv4.1 or 4.2 (the default) on a reachable tcp/2049. Impact: one TCP connection writes 61 bytes past a kernel heap object; chained, that gives a root shell. Now: patch and reboot. Until then, firewall tcp/2049. Key facts Severity 9.8 Critical (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N) Attack Remote, unauthenticated, tcp/2049 Impact Kernel heap overflow → remote root shell Bug age 12 years, since Linux 3.16 (2014) Affected In-kernel nfsd with NFSv4.1 or 4.2 Fixed in 6.12.117 · 6.18.61 · 7.3.2 · 7.4-rc1 One connection, no login # The NFS server runs inside the kernel and parses network input before it knows who you are. CVE-2026-99362 lives in that gap: a client can shrink its reply cache to zero bytes, then make the server copy a full reply into it. The copy lands on the kernel heap, and the client picks most of the bytes. How NFS2ROOT reaches a Linux NFS server: one unauthenticated TCP connection to port 2049 Twelve years in a few lines of C # Timeline Mar 2014 Commit 47ee52986472 narrows the reply buffer while handling SEQUENCE . It ships in Linux 3.16. 2014 to 2026 12 years Every kernel since 3.16 carries it: LTS, distribution and appliance kernels. 17 Aug 2026 Jérémy Jean of ANSSI sends a fix upstream with a KASAN report. 21 Sep 2026 OpenSec's Antara flags the bug, scores it 9.8 and turns it into a root shell on its own. 20 Nov 2026 CVE-2026-99362 is published with fixes. Watch it run # A real run, end to end. Left: the victim's console. Right: our client on another machine, talking to the victim only over tcp/2049. NFS2ROOT recording: an unauthenticated client gets a root shell on a Linux NFS server The overflow. The kernel warns in nfsd4_check_resp_size , but the out-of-bounds copy has already happened. Root. The attacker hangs up, and the victim's kernel runs our command: root , then uid=0(root) , then power-off. Root cause # Each NFSv4.1 session slot caches its last reply, so a retried request is answered exactly once. The client decides how big that cache is. Set it to the minimum and every slot's buffer is zero bytes. nfsd4_sequence() then shrinks the reply buffer to that limit before it accepts the slot. Pad the request's tag so the buffer fills right after the SEQUENCE opcode, and the encoder quits without flagging an error. The server believes SEQUENCE succeeded and caches the whole reply, headers and tag included, into a buffer with room for nothing. KASAN report from

articles.title: SSH is a GUI framework
articles.content: SSH is a GUI framework Hasan Madi · 21 November 2026 "One thing about which fish know exactly nothing is water." — Marshall McLuhan SSH is a tool so ubiquitous that we've forgotten what it actually is: a multiplexed, encrypted byte stream accessible on a cross-platform rendering engine that ships on every laptop, server, and phone on earth. A number of terminal protocols have slowly added graphics, clipboard sharing (including images), notifications, mouse support, and more on top of SSH. To see just how far you can push it, I've made a microVM with a desktop environment designed from the ground up to render natively over SSH. You can try it right now (no sign-up): ssh zydra.sh ssh -p 443 zydra.sh # if on an office network ssh -t zydra.sh dino # SSH port of the Chromium T-Rex game, for fun. zydra.sh desktop, entirely over SSH, in the Kitty terminal Terminal Protocols (and matching terminal support) All terminal protocols work on data that can be passed through SSH, so typically, any terminal protocol will extend to SSH. Perhaps the most ubiquitous new terminal protocol is the Kitty Graphics Protocol , which superseded the older Sixel and iTerm2 graphics protocols. It allows for compression, client-side graphical state (via VRAM), and even animations entirely on the terminal. Graphics alone don't make a complete GUI, though. SSH has protocols that cover all other angles: Notifications : OSC 99 "Rich Notifications" allow image, text, and body. OSC 777 (our first fallback) allows only text and body, and OSC 9 (our last fallback) allows only a title. We end up using a similar fallback for many things. Clipboard sharing : OSC 52 handles bidirectional clipboard sharing, and Kitty's OSC 5522 adds image and arbitrary MIME-type transfers on top of that. Mouse support : CSI ? 1000-1006 help track the mouse and give us its precise coordinates. Synchronized Output (Batched Rendering): CSI ? 2026 allows atomic rendering, preventing visual tearing and flickering. File upload (Kitty) : The Kitty terminal uniquely supports a file upload feature, which zydra.sh uses to allow the upload of projects and related files to personal VMs. SSH-native compositing: How I made it fast A few tricks make compositing over SSH fast. Firstly, where possible, especially when streaming terminals, we simply stream them as text rather than unnecessarily streaming it via graphics. The compositor's UI framework itself cleverly overlays traditional text over carefully aligned graphics, saving bandwidth. In the case of zydra.sh , this allows us to efficiently stream the entire cloud computer's desktop UI over SSH. Next, we optimize graphics by sending a sort of "grid" of pixels. Each cell has its own updates, where the previous frame is compared to the current frame to catch and send updates, avoiding having to constantly stream the full screen. articles.title: Optimizing Rustc's next trait solver
articles.content: The next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0. In the last stages, before stabilizing it, its performance was a major blocker. But what is "a trait solver"? And why is its performance a problem? My goal for this blog post is to answer those questions in a way where you don't need any prior knowledge. I think discussions of the trait solver can quickly become quite involved, and daunting. So today, we'll start from the very basics! This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026. And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube: VIDEO The new solver is the codebase I work on daily, and I've done so for about a year full-time. I'm not the main person driving its stabilization though, that would be lcnr , who's worked on it for far longer than I've been around in the Rust project. My main focus has been optimizing the new solver's performance. Many people have worked avery hard, for years, to make the new solver a reality. You can find some of them here , and here . My work here is only possible because of Hexcat and RustNL paying me and others to work on rust compiler development. Consider whether you or your company could sponsor Hexcat or the RustNL maintainer team . History of the new solver On the 15th of May, 2015, Rust reached a major milestone. The very first stable version of rust was released. Version 1.0.0 . Just 72 days later, on the 24th of July, work started on a new trait solver. Or well, that's when the Chalk project got its first commit. It seems the initial goal was to formalize the trait system so we could prove its correctness. One reason that didn't work well is because the trait system wasn't very correct at all. Chalk is, according to its github description, "An implementation and definition of the Rust trait system using a PROLOG-like logic solver". The fact that it's "PROLOG-like" we'll come back to in a few paragraphs, it's quite interesting! However, Chalk isn't around anymore. Its README.md says it has been "sunset in favor of the newer next-generation trait solver". In October 2022, this project was officially started to turn the lessons learned from Chalk, into an actual new subsystem of the rust compiler, that, once finished, could replace the code of the old trait solver. The goal of the new trait solver is to make sure we wouldn't have as many correctness bugs in the trait system. We now call this project "project zero" , referring to the number of soundness bugs we'd ideally like to have in our type system. There have been several very long standing bugs in Rust's (old) trait solver. Like this one , that has been open since May 28, 2015 (just 13 days after Rust 1.0!). articles.title: Abolish Lock Poisoning
articles.content: Abolish Lock Poisoning written on November 25, 2026 Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning. When some Rust code panics while holding a std::sync::Mutex , the mutex is poisoned . That means that any further call to lock() returns a PoisonError . The motivation for this feature is that an object might have some internal invariants that need to be upheld and panicking in the wrong moment might invalidate reasonable at and leave an object behind in a broken state. Personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me. The libs team is discussing making the non-poisoning locks the default in the next edition but entirely expectedly it has caused quite a few people to jump to the defence of the feature. In this post I want to make my personal case why poisoned locks should either be entirely removed or be made the exception. Primarily this is because I have yet to come across code in the wild that handles a poisoned lock correctly. On the other hand I have come across enough code that mishandles it and as a result behaves worse than a parking_lot lock would which does not support poisoning. Josh Triplett put it quite strongly in a hackernews comment: “In the entire history of the standard library, we have never once seen a single report of anyone attempting to recover from poison.” When a panic happens with a lock held, there are two reasonable reactions: shut the process down, or carry on and ignore the flag. With panic = "abort" you get the former and poisoning never comes up. From all the evidence I have seen, with unwinding, the idiomatic lock().unwrap() picks the worst option of all. That’s because it neither stops the process nor lets it continue as it will turn every further lock into a panic with sometimes disastrous effects. But that is not the only issue with the system today. So here I want to share some of the issues and with some references to real world code of how people got bitten. The Error Holds the Lock One subtle aspect to the poisoning is that the PoisonError needs to hold the guard. That’s because in order to ignore the poison flag, you need to fetch the guard from the error object. Holding on to the error means holding on to the lock! That can cause common code that does error wrapping / error conversions into a deadlock hazard. The innocent looking m.lock()? in a function returning Box<dyn Error> or similar keeps the mutex locked for as long as the error lives ( #159930 ). This can also happen with if let. For instance in cc-switch you can see that they had a test hung because a if let Ok(..) = lock() { .. } else { .. } fallback locked the same mutex again while the unnamed PoisonError from the condition still owned the guard. PC-AI had the same bug in a match arm. Another case can be found in ox-embed-server . Panic To Outage Deviously poisoning does not fail fast and done wro

articles.title: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
articles.content: Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone. But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine. This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox. As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU. Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test. Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed. One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step. That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen. The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door. Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

articles.title: Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each
articles.content: Elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone. A common DNS mistake can leave them open for attackers to grab, which can lead to credential theft and worse. We demonstrated the attack is still possible in 2026, including finding real takeovers on US treasury domains, which were reported and fixed via a bug bounty program. The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain! We only covered less than 1% of the total IP space, so there are many more out there for attackers to grab. So, now is the time to review your DNS records and get those dangling records squashed ASAP. As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost. Practical EIP takeover To test how exploitable it is to claim the AWS host that a dangling DNS record points to, we needed to find a way to cycle through available EIPs with automation. The full EIP space is a maximum of ~80 million IP addresses (in practice, probably half that), and these are allocated at random, so you can’t simply claim the IP address that you want. To do this, we’d need to repeatedly allocate and release Elastic IPs from AWS’s EC2 pool, and check each address against the DNS records in our scope. Targets We wanted to report any dangling records we found, so we built our target list from public bug bounty scopes. Using the bbscope API, we pulled wildcard scope entries and passed them into subfinder to enumerate subdomains. We resolved the A records for each host and stored anything not in private or reserved ranges in a DynamoDB table for use later in our pipeline. Claiming Addresses By default, a new AWS account can hold five Elastic IPs per region. The loop works with five, but a higher quota means more addresses per cycle. Since Service Quotas automatically approves an increase to 25 Elastic IPs per region without a support case, we requested the increase in every region. With the quota increased, we ran a Python script to claim addresses with each cycle following this flow: Allocate 25 Elastic IPs in the current region. Store each address, checking for duplicates. Look up each address in the database. Keep and log any address that matches a target’s A record. Release every address that didn’t match. Move to the next region and repeat. In a single region, releasing and immediately allocating a new IP often returned the same address, suggesting AWS recycles recently released addresses first. Rotating through regions gave each pool time to move on, so by the time the tool returned to the original region, it would be allocated a fresh set of IPs. articles.title: Entering the Geminispace
articles.content: On May 1st, 2020, Project Gemini made the rounds for the first time via a Hacker News discussion thread . I remember seeing the announcement back then, barely a month after the Covid 19 worldwide lockdown, and thinking it was a cool gimmick. But that was that. However, I’ve recently been seeing a few gemini:// links here and there as footers in hand-crafted blogs, and I nerd-snipped myself to export this blog as a Gemini capsule that you can find at gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/ . The process has been fun, and I actually quite like the extreme minimalism of the resulting site. So what else would you expect from me? I had to write about it—hence this post. Today we’ll learn a little bit about what Gemini is, how I approached the blog export to its native gemtext format, and I’ll confess a couple of… sins I committed along the way. A blog on operating systems, programming languages, testing, build systems, my own software projects and even personal productivity. Specifics include FreeBSD, Linux, Rust, Bazel and EndBASIC. What is Gemini? A terrible name, that is. Looking for information about Gemini these days is extremely hard, thanks to Google polluting the namespace with its own AI offering. Of course that’s not Project Gemini’s fault because Google’s thing came after them, but still, good luck finding stuff about this network. Joking aside, let’s look at Project Gemini’s barebones front page: Project Gemini's front page, displayed in the Lagrange browser. … and break down the introductory and only paragraph: Gemini is a new internet technology supporting an electronic library of interconnected text documents. You can think of Gemini as a way to access a bunch of text-only pages, with links among them, so you can find information and follow links to additional resources. Instead of using http:// or https:// URL prefixes, you use gemini:// instead. That’s not a new idea, but it’s not old fashioned either. Exactly. articles.content: New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: CNCF 与 Linux 基金会研究显示虚拟机承载约 53% 生产应用，AI 与智能体负载进一步推高虚拟化需求。

articles.title: OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando
articles.content: OpenAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The company reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches. By Eran Stiller
articles.summary: OpenAI 推出 Git 后端 Pando，支持并发编码智能体工作流，推送延迟中位数降低近 80%。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #544: AI is now the most-cited risk in the Fed's survey: 87%, up from 50%
articles.content: The Federal Reserve asked its market contacts what could shake the financial system, and 87% named AI, up from 50% in the spring. The same week, the FAA halted flights nationwide days after putting an AI tool in every regional control center, and says it is still looking at what happened. Nvidia's board has approached Arm's CEO about replacing Jensen Huang. Russian pranksters got three OpenAI national security staff on a video call. In the middle: Anthropic prices its IPO on Wednesday with $900.9 billion in compute commitments on its books.
articles.summary: 美联储调查中 87% 受访者将 AI 列为最受关注风险，较春季的 50% 大幅上升。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #543: Google is the latest tech giant to chase TypeSafe's 8-week-old Jev
articles.content: This issue is about decision models, a new kind of AI model that does not write text. You give it an input and a fixed list of answers, and it returns the best answer with a probability, in milliseconds. TypeSafe AI released the first one, Jev, on September 15. On Wednesday Google released its own, after OpenAI and Microsoft did in October, and all three charge $0.10 or less per million input tokens and nothing for output. Shanghai AI Lab says its 4B model beat Jev on its tests, and Microsoft built its model on Alibaba's Qwen. Chatbots still score a little higher on the hardest decisions, at 15 times the cost. In the middle: on Vercel's gateway, decision models took one in four AI requests in October.
articles.summary: TypeSafe AI 于9月15日发布决策模型 Jev，输入问题与候选答案即可毫秒级返回最优解；谷歌本周跟进推出同类模型，巨头竞逐新型AI模型。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: 本周日程密集：美国36州州长选举中，最多15场支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人有望胜出；苹果、AMD财报及苹果测试动态同步进行。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: 美联储利率决议后微软、Alphabet周三发布财报，亚马逊周四跟进；投资者关注AI投入回报，CoreWeave债务违约保险成本飙升引发信贷担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: 基于用例库与SEC文件分析，AI发现安全漏洞的速度已超团队修复能力，部分公司AI代理承担大量工作，测试代理持续增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 据纽约时报，竞选团队与PAC在中期选举AI生成广告上花费超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注AI；某超级PAC向仅存邮箱地址的内华达公司支付约2000万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备；本期还汇总了专家最关注的链接，包括一项大型研究。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 专家分享聚焦：顶尖AI模型未能通过自主开展AI研究的测试，同时涉及AI治理话语权、军事规划应用及进入个人电脑等议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: 近三周企业AI实践显示：因成本过高，公司纷纷转向更便宜的模型；大型部署已进入日常使用，同时AI被限制或撤除的场景增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务；剑桥因AI训练条款拒绝Turnitin新协议，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，格里芬向卡内基梅隆捐赠30亿美元。

articles.title: Warp bets on the software factory
articles.content: Zach Lloyd, founder and CEO of Warp, is back to talk about what he calls the company's primary bet: Warp Factories, open infrastructure for running a cloud software factory, which he calls the new version of CI/CD. He explains factory as code, what's inside an agent trace, why self-improving systems drift, and how his senior engineers went from guardians of the code to the biggest adopters once the models got good enough. Then he and Adam get into whether this is a pivot, why the best interface might be no new interface at all, coding as a team in Slack, and Adam's case for continuous flow.
articles.summary: Warp CEO Zach Lloyd介绍公司核心押注Warp Factories：运行云端软件工厂的开放基础设施，称其为CI/CD新形态，并讲解工厂即代码与代理追踪。

articles.title: A seminal moment in computing
articles.content: MG, founder and CEO of WorkOS, is back to talk about leading a company through what DHH called a seminal moment in computing. He explains Atlas, the AI coworker WorkOS built for itself and then launched, why agents will soon choose and sign up for your tech stack, and why this moment feels closer to fire than to the iPhone. Then he gets practical: starting a company is easier than ever, but product-market fit is harder, so be a heat-seeking missile for pain, pick customers you like, and stop calling yourself non-technical.
articles.summary: WorkOS CEO MG谈带领公司度过计算领域关键时刻，介绍自研AI同事Atlas，并预测代理将自主选择并注册技术栈。

articles.title: Orbin' with Amp
articles.content: Quinn Slack is back and we're talking about the next level for Amp. Agents write the code, they review the code, and they can push it to main (like our friends at Amp). But where should your agents live? Who remembers what you actually asked them to do? Amp is now its own company, and Quinn has a lot to say about orbs, threads that last forever, and why code review as we know it is fading. He explains why the model matters less than it used to, and why he worries we could lose the open source commons. Quinn even built a feature request live on the show to solve my tailnet problem.
articles.summary: Amp独立成公司，Quinn Slack介绍代理编写、审查并推送代码的新阶段，探讨代理应部署何处及如何记住用户指令。

articles.title: All your packages are belong to us
articles.content: AI agents can write the code, choose the packages, and run the install. Who's checking what they just invited onto your machine? This week I'm joined by Ahmad Nassri, CTO of Socket and former CTO of npm. We get into the trust built into a package install, the new ways attackers are using agents, and what it takes to keep building without handing over the keys or your wallet.
articles.summary: Socket CTO、前npm CTO Ahmad Nassri探讨AI代理自动选包安装带来的供应链信任风险，以及攻击者利用代理的新手法。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr回顾其“黑客定律”项目，指出团队当前瓶颈是让所有人的心智模型与实际构建保持同步，主持人当场称之为“Kerr定律”。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens谈Postgres生态扩张：核心刻意保持简单、扩展繁荣，pg_lake引入DuckDB与Iceberg，并讨论ETL痛点与AI对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha谈将“无聊”的邮件服务扩展至300万用户、背后的Go重写、面向代理的构建，以及pricing.md、MCP与垃圾邮件团伙。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: Gavriel Cohen讲述40小时周末项目NanoClaw如何成为爆款开源项目并发展为AI公司，因安全顾虑打造容器隔离的OpenClaw替代方案。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 在播客中提出开源仓库可能已被大规模攻陷的猜想，并讨论 AI 如何压缩知识图谱。

articles.title: World Has Six Consecutive Days 2C Above Preindustrial Levels For First Time
articles.content: Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating. The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days. "This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning," said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. "The CO2 increase from this year to next will be about 3.5 parts per million, a third faster than in recent years and nearly twice as fast as what it should have been limited to if we'd been on track to limit global warming to 1.5C." Zeke Hausfather, a climate researcher at Berkeley Earth, said: "Another day, another global temperature record," adding that the previous record of 2.05C over the 1850-1900 baseline, set in 2023, has been "smashed." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 全球首次出现连续六天较工业化前升温超过2°C，虽属短暂纪录，但凸显气候临界风险。

articles.title: Suspected Chinese Agents Are Trying to Dupe Americans with Fake Listings on Job Platforms
articles.content: "LinkedIn is probably the greatest intelligence tool that's ever been created," CNN heard from Holden Triplett, director of counterintelligence at the National Security Council in the first Trump administration. A LinkedIn spokesperson responded that "Creating a fake account or misrepresenting your identity is a clear violation of our terms of service." (And they also told CNN that LinkedIn remains "focused on detecting state-sponsored abuse and will continue to enforce our policies against fake accounts.") But it's not just happening on LinkedIn... Suspected Chinese spies have created an elaborate web of fake firms with job opportunities aimed at tricking current and former US officials into divulging government secrets as part of a scheme that is more pervasive than previously reported, CNN has found. Interviews with a dozen people caught up in the operation — as well as CNN analysis of suspected bogus websites — reveal how there is a much broader target pool for obtaining sensitive US information after the Trump administration laid off thousands of federal employees. [CNN reported in 2025 that "foreign powers such as China and Russia" had directed their intelligence services "to ramp up recruiting of Americans working in national security by targeting those who had been fired or felt they were at risk of losing their jobs".] These workers left their posts with inadequate guidance and protection from spying plots, ex-officials said, creating a potentially valuable resource for Beijing and weak spot for Washington... In addition to government workers, the plot has targeted journalists, trade consultants and others, who might have knowledge deemed valuable to US adversaries. The FBI offered a glimpse into the malicious recruiting scam when it seized 13 websites officials say were tied to fake consulting firms in June. China denied the FBI allegations. articles.summary: 报道称疑似中国特工在 LinkedIn 等招聘平台发布虚假职位诱骗美国人，平台方回应将打击虚假账号。

articles.title: Anthropic, OpenAI Employees Fear Models Are Too Unsafe to Ever Release
articles.content: Axios reports: Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem: Internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates... The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen, sources told Axios. Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some insiders believe it's fixable. Others aren't convinced and say companies should stop training new models entirely... Anthropic and OpenAI have unreleased models that are far more powerful than what they've already released publicly, but the AI companies have struggled to ensure that they are safe enough for public release, sources said. This has led to debate within Anthropic, OpenAI and the AI research community about whether to stop releasing future frontier models publicly, instead reserving them for internal deployment only. There has also been debate around whether to train new models at all, sources inside and outside those companies told Axios. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 据二十余名知情人士，Anthropic 与 OpenAI 内部未发布模型能力过强，部分员工担忧其无法安全对外发布。

articles.title: Saudi National Charged In OpenAI Bugging To Be Released On $1 Million Bond
articles.content: CNBC reports: Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an OpenAI executive conference room, will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday. Alfozan, 35, is expected to be released on Wednesday and be fitted with an ankle monitor, according to his attorney, David Rizk... [U.S. District Court Magistrate Judge Alex Tse] ruled in favor of a release motion by Rizk filed last week that said prosecutors had admitted they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia." The San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office opposed the former OpenAI engineer's release, saying in its response that he remains a flight risk due to his "considerable resources and ties to Saudi Arabia." Alfozan's release request "blithely dismisses the seriousness" of the charge he faces, and "appears to presume, without support, that the government's investigation is complete," prosecutors wrote... Prosecutors said they have found hundreds of audio files on Alfozan's personal computer, "including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, many of which involve discussions of what may be trade secrets." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 被控在 OpenAI 高管会议室安装窃听设备的沙特籍男子获准以100万美元保释，并将佩戴电子监控。

articles.title: Tuesday Jensen Huang Said Nvidia Doesn't Need a Succession Plan, and that He's in Therapy
articles.content: CNBC reports: [Jensen Huang] told staff that Nvidia has built a team that doesn't require succession planning the way a normal organization does, because the company operates a unique business model where there are multiple capable leaders at Nvidia that are leading different parts of the organization. A succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy, Huang said, according to one of the people present... Huang told staff that Tuesday's company meeting was the second hardest meeting of his life, the first one being with his wife. He said he is in therapy, according to one of the people present. The Independent notes that Jensen Huang told Nvidia's board Sunday "that he had more affairs beyond the two that were already in the public domain, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter." Huang was reportedly "contrite" about his behavior during the crunch talks, and the board discussed "the importance of candor and honesty" with him, according to the newspaper. Elsewhere CNBC reports even President Trump's "staunchest allies" in the U.S. Congress "recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang..." "The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States...." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 黄仁勋对员工表示英伟达有多位能干的领导者分管不同业务，无需传统接班计划，并透露自己在接受心理治疗。

articles.title: FAA Identifies Patches for Last Week's Flight-Grounding Router Issue. But Was Staffing an Issue?
articles.content: CNN published an exclusive report Tuesdayon what caused last week's nationwide ground stop for flights in the U.S.. A source familiar with the Federal Aviation Administration's investigation says they've recreated the issue in a lab "and believe they found the culprit." Investigators have focused on determining why a new router at a remote Arkansas radio site overwhelmed the nation's air traffic control system with a massive amount of data, triggering gaps in radar and radio communications. They found an overlooked router setting affected how it interfaced with other decades-old routers that the FAA is decommissioning, the source said. Investigators believe software updates are needed and that those patches will prevent a repeat of the system failure... This month's ground stop not only focused attention on upgrades being made to the aging system, which have been paused as the agency investigated the incident, but also raised questions about FAA oversight of private companies charged with maintaining the network... On the day of the network meltdown, L3Harris was undertaking a maintenance job that involved switching the system from a decades-old router to a new one. In the past, this kind of work typically involved at least six FAA employees. Under the Trump administration, it's now often coordinated by one employee: an FAA liaison. And there are only four people in the country with that title, according to sources familiar with the process. The liaison's job involves coordinating and scheduling these upgrades — not approving them, sources said... The Trump administration's effort to move maintenance work along faster also eliminated a layer of FAA review that was critical to assessing risk [according to a source familiar with the process]. Previously, local technical operations managers, site technicians and others would determine when the work could be done with the least impact on air traffic and to game out worst-case scenarios. articles.summary: FAA 称已在实验室复现上周导致全美航班停飞的路由器故障并锁定补丁，同时调查人员配置是否为诱因。

articles.title: Huawei Is Guilty of Conspiracy To Steal Trade Secrets, a US Jury Finds
articles.content: The Associated Press reports: A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiring to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks. But jurors acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy, a result that the company's lawyer said was a "profound rejection" of the government's narrative that it was corrupt from top to bottom and had a corporate culture of cheating, stealing and lying. Prosecutors had used the charge, commonly found in organized crime and drug cases, to accuse Huawei of operating illicitly to poach intellectual property and technological secrets from competitors and partners. The convictions covered allegations that the company did business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions — including Iran and North Korea — and made false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds. In all, Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 counts. The case in Brooklyn federal court involved no human defendants, but the company could be made to pay billions of dollars in penalties when it is sentenced next September... Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in "economic bullying" and improperly used national security as a pretext for oppressing Chinese companies. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Maze-Maker: Square, circle, triangle, hexagon, star and heart mazes with seven algorithms
articles.content: Make a maze right in your browser: square, round, triangular, hexagonal, star or heart-shaped, with long winding corridors or a thicket of short dead ends. Then find your way through it with the arrow keys or a finger, or watch the solution draw itself, and save it as an SVG or a PNG, or print it. No sign-up and no libraries. A maze is a puzzle: it has branches and dead ends, and a way through. (A labyrinth has a single path and no choices; for those, see Labyrinth-Maker .) Shapes : Square : a grid, entered at the top left and left at the bottom right. Circle : rings of cells, entered from the outside with the goal at the center. Triangle : a big triangle cut into small triangular cells, entered and left at the bottom corners. Hexagon : a honeycomb of hexagonal cells, each with up to six neighbors, entered on the left corner and left on the right one. Star : a six-pointed star cut from the triangle grid, so its edges stay straight, entered at the top of the upper left point and left under the lower right point. Heart : a square grid cut to the shape of a heart, entered at the top of the left lobe and left at the tip. Algorithms : recursive backtracker, Prim, Kruskal, Wilson, Hunt & Kill, Growing Tree and Aldous-Broder. Each one gives mazes of a different texture. Size and loops : from 6 to 60 cells across. Loops opens a share of the dead ends, so there is more than one way through. Solution length : Any, Short, Medium or Long. The app makes a dozen mazes from the seeds that follow and keeps the one with the shortest, the middle or the longest way through. Seed : every maze comes from a number. The same settings and seed always give the same maze, and the page address keeps them, so a link brings back the same maze. Solve it : move with the arrow keys or WASD, or drag the dot. Backing up erases your trail. Show solution draws the shortest way through. Look : five color schemes (paper, blueprint, hedge, stone, night), wall thickness, and coloring by distance from the entrance. Save : Download PNG (2000 pixels square), Download SVG , or Print (black on white, maze only). Start with every wall standing, and knock walls down until every cell can be reached, but never so many that a loop appears: in graph terms, a spanning tree of the grid. The result is a perfect maze, with exactly one path between any two cells. The algorithms differ in the order they pick walls: Backtracker (depth-first search) carves as far as it can before backing up: long corridors, few dead ends. Prim grows the maze out from one cell: many short dead ends. Kruskal joins random regions anywhere on the grid: an even texture. Wilson uses loop-erased random walks, so every possible maze is equally likely. Hunt & Kill walks like the backtracker, but when stuck it hunts for a new cell next to the maze instead of backing up. articles.title: Sometimes three boring statements beats one clever expression
articles.content: Modern JavaScript gives us a lot of expressive tools. Sometimes a little too many. Optional chaining, nullish coalescing, ternaries, spread, template literals. I like all of them and use them every day. But together, they make it really easy to cram a lot of logic into a single expression. I used to think that was a sign of good JavaScript. I’m not so sure anymore. When one more ?? is too many Take something like this: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? defaults.theme; I’ve written this plenty of times. It’s short and it works. But once these expressions start growing, they read more like puzzles than code: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? getFallbackTheme() ?? defaults.theme; I can follow it, but I have to stop and parse it. Compare that to this: let theme = config?.theme; if (theme == null) { theme = user?.preferences?.theme; } if (theme == null) { theme = getFallbackTheme(); } return theme ?? defaults.theme; More lines? Sure. But it’s a lot more obvious. Yes, I give up const and reassign a variable. I’ll take that trade. Long expressions hide decisions Longer expressions squeeze several decisions into one piece of syntax. The more you chain, the more you have to work out at once: What happens if config is undefined? Where does the fallback come from? Which value wins? What if getFallbackTheme() throws? Chaining saves some vertical space, but you have to hold more in your head. It’s a practical problem, too. You can’t put a breakpoint on one fallback in the middle of a ?? chain, and you can’t log a single step without rewriting the expression. With separate statements, every step gets its own line to stop on or log. The diffs are nicer, as well. Adding a fallback means adding a block, not editing one dense line. Plain statements are fine A lot of us started treating plain if statements as something to avoid. So we’d rather write this: return user?.isAdmin ? getDashboard(user) : getLandingPage(user); than this: if (user?.isAdmin) { return getDashboard(user); } return getLandingPage(user); Neither one is objectively better. The second isn’t “less modern,” it’s often just easier to read. A single ternary like that is fine. It’s when they nest that I stop: return isLoading ? "Loading" : error ? "Failed to load" : items.length === 0 ? "Nothing here yet" : `${items.length} items`; The same thing with plain statements: if (isLoading) return "Loading"; if (error) return "Failed to load"; if (items.length === 0) return "Nothing here yet"; return `${items.length} items`; Clever code gets old fast Over the past couple of years I’ve found myself chaining less and writing fewer nested ternaries. I don’t mind adding another if anymore. I care more about readability than being clever. When I’m debugging production code or reviewing a pull request, I can’t remember ever wishing something had been written as one bigger expression. My rule of thumb is simple. articles.title: Dual JWT Authentication: Security, Redis, and Trade-Offs
articles.content: Authentication is one of those backend features that looks simple until you need to make it secure, scalable, and inexpensive. A user logs in, receives a token, and includes it in subsequent requests. The server verifies the token and allows access. Easy enough. But real applications need more than that. Users expect to stay signed in for weeks, log out from multiple devices, recover from interrupted connections, and have their sessions terminated when credentials are compromised. Meanwhile, backend teams want to avoid unnecessary database queries on every authenticated request. These requirements pull authentication architecture in different directions. One possible compromise is a Dual JWT architecture : short-lived access tokens sent through the Authorization header, longer-lived refresh tokens stored in secure cookies, and a small Redis-backed mechanism for revoking sessions. The approach can reduce database traffic significantly. But its security properties depend on how refresh tokens are managed, how revocation works, and which attacks the application needs to defend against. Let’s examine the architecture, its implementation in Node.js, and the trade-offs that are easy to overlook. 1. Why a Single Token Is Often Not Enough Consider an application that uses one JWT for authentication. After login, the server issues a token: Authorization : Bearer eyJhbGciOi... Every protected API request includes that token. The server verifies its signature and expiration time without querying a session database. This is convenient, but the token’s lifetime creates a problem. If it expires after 15 minutes, users need a way to obtain another token without repeatedly entering their credentials. If it remains valid for 30 days, stealing it may give an attacker access for a long time. Neither option is particularly attractive. What About Cookie-Based Sessions? Traditional session authentication usually stores an opaque session identifier in an HttpOnly cookie. The browser sends that cookie automatically, and the server looks up the associated session. This approach has important advantages. Tokens aren’t exposed to ordinary JavaScript through document.cookie , and individual sessions can be invalidated centrally. However, cookie-based authentication also requires appropriate CSRF defenses because browsers attach eligible cookies automatically. That doesn’t make cookie sessions inherently insecure. Properly implemented server-side sessions remain an excellent choice for many web applications. The question is whether the application needs the additional flexibility of separate access and refresh credentials. 2. Two Tokens, Two Responsibilities The Dual JWT approach separates API access from session renewal. articles.title: 想换一台 MacBook，纠结 14 寸和 16 寸，求有实际使用经验的朋友聊聊
articles.content:
目前手里用的是一台 MacBook Air M2，24GB 内存、1TB 硬盘，平时主要就是办公、浏览网页、看看视频之类的。

一直以来对这台电脑都挺满意的，尤其是便携性。经常需要移动办公，有时候晚上躺在床上抱着电脑看看电视，也不会觉得重。14 寸左右的尺寸对我来说真的刚刚好，轻巧、方便，随时拿起来就能用。

不过之前买电脑的时候，主要考虑的就是日常办公和娱乐，并没有考虑过其他用途。

现在 AI 时代，自己也开始对本地 AI 模型产生兴趣，想折腾一些简单的本地模型，学习、测试一下，另外也会涉及一些代码编译、开发之类的工作。结果发现目前这台 Air 在这些场景下还是有点吃力，性能和散热都有些捉襟见肘。

所以最近有了换电脑的想法。

目前比较纠结的是尺寸问题。

个人还是非常喜欢 14 寸的尺寸，毕竟经常移动办公，也有躺床上使用的习惯，太大太重的话，便携性和使用体验都会打折扣。

但是网上看了不少评测，感觉 15 寸、16 寸的机器在散热、性能释放方面似乎会比 14 寸更有优势。不知道实际使用中差距到底有多大？尤其是长时间跑模型、编译代码这些场景，14 寸和 16 寸的体验会不会有明显区别？

目前个人比较关注 M3 Max 14 寸 MacBook Pro，感觉配置和尺寸似乎都比较符合自己的需求，但又担心 14 寸的散热和持续性能释放不如 16 寸。

想问问论坛里有没有实际使用过 14 寸和 16 寸 MacBook Pro 的朋友，特别是用来跑本地 AI 模型、开发、编译的朋友：

1. 14 寸和 16 寸在散热、持续性能释放方面，实际差距到底有多大？
2. 如果主要是跑一些中小型本地 AI 模型、日常开发和代码编译，14 寸 M3 Max 是否足够？
3. 16 寸除了屏幕大一些，性能和散热方面的优势是否真的值得牺牲便携性？
4. 如果经常移动办公，甚至偶尔躺床上抱着使用，16 寸会不会明显笨重？

目前个人还是更倾向于 14 寸，毕竟便携性对我来说真的很重要，但又不想买回来之后，因为散热或者性能释放的问题而后悔。

希望有实际使用经验的朋友分享一下，尤其是长期使用过这两个尺寸、跑过 AI 模型的朋友，想听听真实体验，而不只是参数和跑分。

先谢谢大家！
articles.summary: V2EX 用户发帖求助，纠结换 14 寸还是 16 寸 MacBook，因本地 AI 模型和开发需求超出 M2 Air 性能，征求实际使用经验。

---

还用了那个 dot，简直就是北美豆包二号，对话几十轮都没给我一次测试脚本。前面一直推，说还在修改不完善不建议上机。跑了一天，动不动就停下来不做了，最后发现版本号已经从 80 升到了 160，就算迭代了 80 个版本也还是不让我实测一下。又过了几轮对话强制要求它给我测试脚本，才勉强给了一个，一看还是获取设备信息（一口老血…）

真的很难理解它的智力

不跑就算了，让它打包，codex 额度快刷新了，准备放本地跑。下载下来发现目录结构大改乱七八糟的，关键也不能用，越改越倒退了

---

上周还没遇到这个问题，即使新会话，上传文档、代码，最多两轮就能进入状态，而且还强烈希望我上机测试给它反馈，这周开始就一直逃避，让它给我成果就一直说问题…

articles.title: 科技爱好者周刊（第 420 期）：最分心的一年
articles.content: 这里记录每周值得分享的科技内容，周五发布。 本杂志 开源 ，欢迎 投稿 。另有 《谁在招人》 服务，发布程序员招聘信息。合作请 邮件联系 （ [email protected] ）。 封面图 新建成的上海道教学院，由清华大学建筑设计研究院设计。（ via ） 最分心的一年 法国开发者 亚历杭德罗·奥 （Alejandro AO），是世界最大的大模型社区 Hugging Face 的布道师。 他做了很多视频，向初学者科普 AI 知识，都放在他的 Youtube 频道 。 他的内容以实操为主，也会涉及一些原理，容易看懂。我很推荐，我的很多 AI 知识就来自这里。 本周，他发布了一篇 年度回顾 ，总结自己在 Hugging Face 的这一年。 引起我共鸣的下面这段话。 他说，2026年是他最分心的一年。"今年几乎不可能专注于一件事。 同时进行多个项目，比以往任何时候都更容易 。大多数时候，我手下有四到十个 Agent 同时推进三四个不同的项目。" 大家有没有同感？ AI 让你可以同时做几件事，越来越难专注于某一件事。 "我每天消耗数百万 Token，尽力做好不同的项目。即使如此，仍然有一些项目被我搁置了。" 他感到，这样是不对的。任何一个项目如果要做到优秀，都需要投入大量时间和心力打磨。分心的直接后果，就是看上去虽然成果不少，但因为时间要分给不同的项目，结果就是每个项目都浅尝辄止，做不深入。 "我们很容易忘记，即使有 AI 编写代码，打造一个可靠的产品也绝非易事。因此，我经常会启动一些看似唾手可得的"小"项目，但这却意味着我推迟了那些我真正想做的、更有意义的项目。而这些小项目最终耗费的时间比预期要多得多。" AI 让人产生一种错觉，觉得只要稍微花一点点时间，构思一下提示词，就能拿到结果。于是，你就抵不住诱惑，只要脑子里蹦出的点子，都忍不住让 AI 去实现，从而将注意力从那些高优先级、急迫而重要的事情上移开。 更糟糕的是，那些你以为最多只需要一个小时的小项目，结果不断膨胀，吞噬了比预想多得多的时间。 正确的做法是，永远不要忘记， AI 可以让事情变得简单，但不会让时间变多 。你每天的时间永远只有24个小时，并行的事情越多，就意味着每件事分到的时间就越少，就做不到把足够的时间花在最重要的事情上面。 你的目标不是去做很多事情，而是做成最重要的事情。 AI 越发达，每件事看上去越容易推进，就越需要我们抵制住诱惑。你要始终划分事件的优先级，筛选掉那些低优先级的事情，让工作范围更聚焦。始终把最多的时间和精力，放在最重要的事情上面。 亚历杭德罗·奥最后许愿，希望2027年不再那么分心，更专注于自己那一两个核心项目。 这也是我对自己的愿望，与其做加法（用 AI 做更多的事情），不如做减法（减少项目数量），借助 AI 把最重要的项目做得更大、更广、更深入。 《GTA6》的写实主义 《GTA5》是史上最畅销的 3A 游戏，卖出了2亿多份。它的续作《GTA6》在本周发售。 目前总体上，这个游戏好评如潮，许多玩家都对游戏的写实主义感到震惊。它栩栩如生还原了一个虚拟的充满犯罪的美国大都市（迈阿密）。 不仅街景逼真，而且各种情节也很接近现实。 一个玩家 讲述了自己遇到的情节。 他正在街上开车兜风，看到前面发生了一起交通事故，一辆轿车被卡车从后面撞上。 他赶紧下车查看，卡车司机已经逃之夭夭，轿车司机被困在车里。轿车引擎已经起火了，形势危在旦夕。他将轿车司机从车里拉了出来，后者向他表示感谢，惊恐地说自己差点丧命。 这时，两人发现，肇事的卡车属于商业巨头撒哈拉公司（影射亚马逊公司）。轿车司机立刻说，这是他的机会！他可以起诉撒哈拉，索赔数百万美元。 但是，他需要确凿的身体受伤证明。于是他深吸一口气，回到车里，让火焰烧着了自己的裤子，然后带着烧伤走了出来。 他给律师打了电话。接着，救护车驶近时，他转过身来，请求那位玩家做他的证人，作为交换，他会给玩家一部分赔偿金。 玩家当时想过要不要向他勒索更多的金额，但最终还是答应帮忙。轿车司机就通过游戏里的货币，给玩家转了几千美元。 这个游戏就是设定这样的情节。 一句话消息 1、美国北卡罗来纳州的 两个男子 突发奇想，将两部电动滑板车绑在一起，然后把家里的沙发固定在滑板车上，变成了一辆沙发车。 他们就坐在沙发上，操作着滑板车的把手，上街闲逛。毫不意外，很快就被警察拦下了。 这件事报道后，引起了轰动。警察局接受采访，解释了为什么沙发车不能上街。首先，它不安全；其次，其他司机看到它会分心，导致危险驾驶。 2、科学家在西班牙发了一具 梁龙化石 ，人们以前一直认为这种恐龙只生活在北美洲。 这表明，至少在这头恐龙生活的时代（1.5亿年前），西欧和北美之间是有陆地通道的，大西洋是后来形成的。 3、为什么黑猩猩没有进化成人？最新一项 研究 ，提出了一种可能的原因。 研究发现，700万年前出现了一种病毒，影响了黑猩猩的大脑发育，使其无法进化出智能，而人类对这种病毒免疫。 这给人的感觉是，好险啊。要是这个病毒再高明一点，把人类也感染了，那岂不是就没有人类社会了。 文章 1、 黄仁勋事件的深层分析 （英文） 一位美国分析师对黄仁勋事件的长篇分析，写得非常深入，值得一读。 2、 多智能体系统的三种模式 （英文） 如果你同时使用多个 AI 代理，本文认为有三种使用模式：（1）管道式（做完一步移交给下一步），（2）编排式（通过编排器来指挥），（3）白板式（每个 AI 自己阅读白板信息，自由行动）。 3、 检查空格有多难？ （英文） 空白字符在 Unicode 有多种表示方法，本文介绍在 Python、Java、JavaScript 里面想要过滤所有空白字符要怎么做。 4、 闭源模型占据了主导地位 （英文） 自从美国的模型公司对低端模型降价以后，几乎在每个价位上，都是闭源模型提供更好的性能。 5、 个人如何定制芯片 （英文） 本文介绍，美国出现了一个网站 wafer.space ，可以接受个人的芯片订单，帮你生产出来（流片）。它的最小订购量是1000片，每片最低价格2美元。 6、 AI 芯片的位置验证 （英文） 为了阻止中国获得先进芯片，美国打算立法要求芯片制造商加入定位功能，可以看到芯片在哪里使用，但是这个功能需要操作系统配合。 工具 1、 sgrep grep 的替代品，返回语义搜索的结果。 2、 Netdata 开源仪表板，在一个地方显示所有服务器和服务的状态。 3、 FlowVision macOS 的瀑布式图像浏览器。 4、 13ft 一个开源网站，可以抓取付费墙后面的网页内容，需要自搭建。 5、 netboot.xyz 一个操作系统的启动盘，把 Windows、Linux、BSD 的安装文件都做在一个启动盘里面。 6、 Srcbook 类似于 Jupyter Notebook 的网页互动式笔记本，但是适用于 TypeScript 和 JavaScript。 7、 Photoshot 开源的基于浏览器的图片编辑器。（ @Abraham721 投稿） 8、 XJY Editor 一个纯静态的网页应用，采用表格形式可视化编辑 XML / KML / JSON / YAML 文件。（ @lizhaowu-79 投稿

articles.title: 科技爱好者周刊（第 419 期）：机房来了，写字楼走了
articles.content: 这里记录每周值得分享的科技内容，周五发布。 本杂志 开源 ，欢迎 投稿 。另有 《谁在招人》 服务，发布程序员招聘信息。合作请 邮件联系 （ [email protected] ）。 封面图 成都麓湖生态城的 Q8 步行桥，采用双曲线造型，在机动车桥的下方穿过，盘旋处形成一个湖心岛。（ via ） 机房来了，写字楼走了 前几天，我看到一个短视频。有个博主来到内蒙古乌兰察布，拍下自己看到的景象，非常震惊。 那里现在是真正的"热土"，曾经的草原遍布工地，聚集了几万个建筑工人，到处都在开工建设机房。 你敢相信吗？一个内陆地级市，最新统计是已经有100多个数据中心（包括建设中），全国主要 IT 公司和算力公司几乎都在那里有自己的机房。乌兰察布已经成了我国算力战略的重点城市。 它的成因，那个博主总结了几点，说得挺好。 （1）离北京近。它跟北京的直线距离约240公里，光纤往返延迟仅4.2毫秒。 （2）绿电丰富。它的有效风场面积占全国十分之一，年日照超3200小时，风电和太阳能根本用不完，导致电价便宜。 （3）气温低。年平均温度4.3度，一年有10个月可以直接利用室外冷空气来散热。 （4）（最初的）地价便宜，一亩才小几万元。当然，现在涨了好多倍。 但是，最打动我的，还是他在短视频结尾说的一句话。 他看着一眼望不到头的机房，脱口而出：" 写字楼会越来越不值钱 ，智力产出正转移到这些数据中心。" 这些新建的数据中心，主要用来跑大模型。随着越来越多的公司广泛使用 AI，很多智力工作会在机房里面完成，那么谁还需要大面积的写字楼？ 再说，任何地方都可以远程调用算力，何必在城市的黄金地段花大价钱租写字楼呢。 我被他的这句话提醒了，意识到了： 机房是新的写字楼，将是智力成果的主要生产场所 ，机房越多，写字的楼需求就越少。 由此看来，城市的办公地产是不看好的，写字楼将过剩，租金下跌。前些年，很多城市都在大建 CBD（中央商务区），以后可能没有这个概念了，乌兰察布那样的"机房之城"才是 AI 时代的 CBD。 奈奎斯特极限 奈奎斯特极限（Nyquist Limit）是信号处理领域的一条定律。 它指的是，如果你想了解一个不断变化的信号， 采样频率必须至少是最高频率的两倍 ，否则就无法准确还原信号。 比如，一个信号每秒变化5次（即频率为5），那么采样频率至少必须是10（即每秒采样10次）。 大家可以参考上图，不同的采样频率（左侧）还原出来的波形不一样（右侧），采样频率越低，失真越大。 有一篇文章 提出， AI 编程也存在奈奎斯特极限 ，代码的改动次数与阅读次数是正比例关系。 阅读代码的频率，必须至少是代码改动频率的两倍，否则无法理解代码。 假设 AI 平均每天改动5次代码，那么你平均每天至少要阅读10次代码（采样），否则很快就会丧失对代码仓库的理解。 大家可以想一想，是不是这样。有些公司为了加快开发速度，不断增加 AI 的使用频率，每天提交大量的代码改动。但是，阅读代码的频率没有同步提升，大大低于奈奎斯特极限（2倍），那么就进入了信号失真状态，他们对自己的产品已经不了解了。 不加密的加密 U 盘 上周，有一件非常尴尬的事情。 国外网友爆出新闻，联想的 加密 U 盘 有问题。 这个 U 盘带有指纹传感器，必须先通过指纹认证，然后才能读写。 网友出于好奇，将这个 U 盘拆开，结果大跌眼镜，里面的存储介质竟然是一块 SD 卡。 取下这块 SD 卡，指纹加密就消失了，卡里的数据不加密就能读写。 难以想象啊，为什么要这么做？加密措施变成了商业噱头。 此外，U 盘里面放 SD 卡，意味着每次读写都要经过双重电路（U 盘电路 + SD 卡电路），性能肯定受影响。而且，SD 卡是不可靠介质，不能用来长期保存数据。 科技动态 1、 流水线键盘 谷歌有一个非常受欢迎的输入法 Gboard ，开发团队在日本，每年10月都要发布一款创意键盘，已经持续了 超过15年 。 前年是一个乌比莫斯环键盘，去年是一个电话拨号转盘键盘。 今年更奇特，居然是流水线键盘。每排按键的下方是一个传送带，所有按键都在传送带上循环滚动。 背后的想法是这样的：打字时，手指需要不停移动，才能按到对应的键。 能不能反过来，手指不动，让键盘动？ 把按键放在传送带上，当它滚动到手指下方时，你往下一按就可以了，整个概念很像回转寿司的滚动带。 这个键盘一共有四条传送带，每条传送带有29个按键。 一旦熟悉以后，用户可以实现不移动手指进行打字，不过打字速度会很感人。 2、 车载泡脚盆 深蓝汽车申请了一项专利，汽车座椅下方可以安装泡脚盆。它自动伸缩，平时缩在座椅里面，需要时乘客用它来泡脚。 根据专利文件，它带有按摩功能，泡脚时盆底的凸起会按摩脚底。另外，还可以配置紫外线模块，进行杀菌。 其实，这个创意挺好的，开长途时，乘客无事可做，正好泡泡脚。 但是，它需要乘客自己注水，然后外接排水管，这意味着车辆必须有储水装置。而且，万一道路颠簸，水还会洒出来，除了搞乱内饰，对电车的风险很大。 3、 树冠桥 巴西的很多公路都穿过亚马逊雨林。野生动物穿过公路时，很容易被车撞到。 一个动物保护组织，就着手在公路两侧的树冠之间架设吊桥，供动物通过。 桥上的摄像头，已经多次拍到了猴子过桥。 这说明，这种公路上方的通道，确实能够保护动物，减少交通事故，还能扩大动物的栖息范围。巴西国会正在通过一项法案，将这种动物通道推广到全国。 文章 1、 我如何阻挡 AI 爬虫访问网站 （英文） 作者的网站流量出现飚升，都是机器人流量。他想了一个办法，在网页中加入一个肉眼不可见的链接，凡是访问该链接的 IP 地址一律自动封禁。 2、 Fable 5.2 一下就生成了我侄子的梦想游戏 （游戏） 小侄子希望作者帮他做一款电子游戏，作为生日礼物。侄子画出了他心目中的游戏草图（下图）。 作者就把这些草图提交给刚发布的 Fable 5.2 模型，大致讲了一下游戏的设想。结果，Fable 5.2 用一个晚上，就生成了所有12个关卡，而且第一次的生成结果就可玩。 3、 币安63亿美元被盗内幕 （英文） 前不久，世界最大加密货币交易平台"币安"被黑客攻破，转走了价值63亿美元的加密货币。本文透露了一些内幕，据说起因是某个币安工程师打算跳槽，找工作面试时，被假冒的雇主欺骗，在笔记本上安装了一个间谍软件。 4、 Node.js 27 的新特性 （英文） 从明年开始，Node.js 每年将只发一个版本，每个版本都是长期支持。2027年的 Node.js 27 版已经在测试了，本文介绍它的新特性。 5、 我放弃 Claude Code，改用 Pi （英文） 作者谈了他对 Claude Code 不满意的地方，导致最后放弃，改用了 Pi 。 6、 黑苹果重生 （英文） 黑苹果指的是将苹果系统移植到非苹果设备上。前几年苹果更换成 M 系列处理器，黑苹果就废了，但是现在 AI 可以帮助移植，黑苹果又慢慢复活，本文举了一些例子。 工具 1、 Window Sweaters for macOS 一个 Mac 应用，为常见应用的窗口穿上毛衣。 2、 dnsglobe 一个命令行工具，对全球34个公共 DNS 进行测速，找出到你速度最快的 DNS 服务器。 3、 ka
